issues.legal_issue: An application to reject a plaint must be decided by reading the plaint as a whole and assessing its pleaded cause of action, rather than by isolating parts of the pleading or relying on the defendant’s version.
material_facts: The defendants sought rejection of the plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action and because the suit was said to be barred by law.
The plaint alleged a continuing tenancy, forcible eviction, and interference with possession and business.
The lower courts rejected the plaint after considering the reliefs and jurisdictional objections.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts were not justified in rejecting the plaint on the basis of the approach they adopted; the plaint had to be considered as a whole, and the suit could not be rejected merely because some reliefs might not be available in the civil court.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order VII Rule 11(a) and (d) of the Code of Civil Procedure, the court considers the plaint’s averments, not the written statement, and reads the plaint meaningfully and as a whole. A real cause of action must be distinguished from an illusory one created by clever drafting. Order VI Rule 2 requires material facts, not evidence; Order VI Rule 16 provides for striking out improper matter, while Order VII Rule 11 does not permit rejection of only part of a plaint. The Court relied on Saleem Bhai v. State of Maharashtra, I.T.C. Ltd. v. Debts Recovery Appellate Tribunal, T. Arivandandam v. T.V. Satyapal, Roop Lal Sathi v. Nachhattar Singh Gill, Raptakos Brett & Co. Ltd. v. Ganesh Property, and Samant N. Balkrishna v. George Fernandez.

predicates.plaint_rejection_proceeding: A party asks the court to reject a plaint for failure to disclose a cause of action or because the suit appears barred by law.
predicates.plaint_read_as_a_whole: The court considers the entire plaint together rather than isolating a sentence, paragraph, or relief.
predicates.pleaded_facts_are_assessed_without_relyi: The court assesses the plaint’s allegations without using the defendant’s written statement to decide the application.

issues.definition: When a court considers rejecting a plaint, it reads the entire plaint and assesses its pleaded facts without relying on the defence, and rejects it only if the whole plaint discloses no cause of action or shows a legal bar.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court may adjudicate a trust tenant’s dispute about the existence and terms of the tenancy even when the plaint also seeks relief concerning the administration of the trust, provided the trust-administration relief is relinquished as directed.
material_facts: The plaintiffs claimed to be tenants of a public trust and disputed whether their tenancy was for eleven years or eleven months.
The plaint sought declarations and protection concerning the tenancy, as well as an inquiry into alleged acts by the trustees.
The plaintiffs were tenants, not persons claiming an interest in the trust.

The Court held that the tenancy dispute was for the civil court, while the trust-administration relief required prior consent under the relevant statutory scheme; it permitted the plaintiffs to apply to relinquish the other reliefs.
issues.conclusion: The plaint was not liable to rejection. The suit could proceed in the civil court on the existence, terms, and duration of the tenancy, subject to the plaintiffs relinquishing the other reliefs as directed.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 50 and 51 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950 govern specified suits concerning trust affairs and require prior consent for a suit of that nature. A tenant of a trust is not a person having an interest in the trust for this purpose, and a dispute about tenancy is not to be decided under Section 50. A claim for relief within the civil court’s jurisdiction is not defeated merely because the plaint also includes a distinct relief that requires the statutory consent. Order II Rules 1 and 2 require claims arising from a cause of action to be included, and the plaintiffs were permitted to relinquish the trust-related reliefs in accordance with law.

rule.if: civil_suit_plaint_rejection_proceeding and tenancy_dispute_between_trust_and_tenant and plaint_also_seeks_trust_administration_relief and tenancy_questions_are_distinct_from_trust_administration_claim and plaintiffs_can_relinquish_the_other_relief

predicates.civil_suit_plaint_rejection_proceeding: A defendant seeks rejection of a plaint filed in a civil suit.
predicates.tenancy_dispute_between_trust_and_tenant: The claimant alleges a tenancy of property held by a trust and the parties dispute the tenancy or its terms.
predicates.plaint_also_seeks_trust_administration_r: The plaint also asks the court to inquire into or grant relief about the administration or affairs of the trust.
predicates.tenancy_questions_are_distinct_from_trus: The tenancy questions can be adjudicated separately from the requested inquiry into the trust’s affairs.
predicates.plaintiffs_can_relinquish_the_other_reli: The claimants can apply to give up the reliefs outside the tenancy dispute.

issues.definition: If a civil plaint concerns a trust tenant’s tenancy and also seeks distinct trust-administration relief that the claimants can relinquish, the plaint is not rejected and the civil suit proceeds only on the tenancy questions.

issues.legal_issue: A person in settled possession who is dispossessed otherwise than in due course of law may sue to recover possession notwithstanding the title asserted against that person.
material_facts: The plaintiffs alleged that they had been forcibly dispossessed despite their continuing tenancy.
The trust disputed the allegation and maintained that possession had been taken lawfully, including by voluntary surrender in some instances.
The Court left the factual dispute about forcible dispossession for consideration by the trial court.
issues.conclusion: A claimant who proves settled possession and dispossession otherwise than in due course of law may seek recovery of possession; whether the plaintiffs were forcibly dispossessed was left for the trial court to decide.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, 1963 permits a person dispossessed from immovable property without consent and otherwise than in due course of law to sue for possession notwithstanding another title. The Court relied on Yashwant Singh v. Jagdish Singh, Krishna Ram Mahale v. Mrs. Shobha Venkata Rao, Ram Rattan v. State of U.P., State of U.P. v. Maharaja Dharmender Prasad Singh, and K.K. Verma v. Union of India.

predicates.summary_possession_suit: The claimant brings a suit seeking recovery of immovable property after being dispossessed.
predicates.claimant_was_in_settled_possession: The claimant had settled possession of the property rather than merely fugitive possession.
predicates.claimant_was_dispossessed_without_consen: The claimant was removed from the property without consent and without use of due legal process.

issues.definition: A claimant in settled possession who is removed without consent and otherwise than through due legal process may seek recovery of the property.

issues.legal_issue: A person in unlawful possession cannot obtain an injunction against the true owner merely to protect that possession.
material_facts: The plaintiffs sought an injunction preventing the trust and its representatives from evicting them or interfering with their possession.
The trust disputed the plaintiffs’ right to remain in possession.
The Court stated the rule concerning an unlawful possessor seeking an injunction against the owner but left the disputed facts about possession and eviction to the trial court.
issues.conclusion: An injunction cannot be granted against the true owner at the instance of a person in unlawful possession; the Court left the factual possession dispute for the trial court.
issues.legal_principle: Injunction is discretionary and judicial proceedings cannot be used to protect or perpetuate a wrong. The Court relied on Mahadeo Savlaram Sheike v. Pune Municipal Corporation, Shiv Kumar Chadha v. MCD, and Dalpat Kumar v. Prahlad Singh.

predicates.injunction_claim: A claimant asks a court to restrain another person from acting in relation to property.
predicates.claimant_is_in_unlawful_possession: The claimant’s possession of the property is unlawful.
predicates.injunction_is_sought_against_true_owner: The person whom the claimant seeks to restrain is the true owner of the property.

issues.definition: A claimant in unlawful possession who seeks an injunction against the true owner cannot obtain that injunction merely to protect the possession.
